# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Review of the 24-Month Varden and Halden Follow-up

This report settles more than any of the earlier documents. It has a registered follow-up, two years of data, a second hours measure that doesn't depend on timesheets, and a pre-specified test of the meetings hypothesis. It also answers several questions I raised earlier: baseline meeting data now appear, waiting times are compared with control offices, and the coverage-bound arm has a clear outcome.

The arithmetic checks out. For example, 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5%, and 0.968 / 0.866 gives +11.8%.

There are problems, though. Two of them affect the headline conclusions. First, it is unclear what the log-measured hours actually count, and this matters for the meetings mechanism. Second, two control offices changed their own practices, which affects the estimated decline in the gain. There is also some overclaiming in how the authors present their vindication.

## 1. What do the log hours count, and does it fit the meetings result?

Log-measured hours are "active log-in time on the county's case-management system". It isn't stated whether this includes time in meetings. The answer matters, because the numbers don't fit together under the most natural reading.

**If logs measure time spent on cases (meetings excluded):**
- At baseline, treated offices worked about 37.9 timesheet hours, of which 7.4 were meetings. That leaves roughly 30.5 hours of non-meeting work.
- At 24 months, timesheet hours are about 12% lower (around 33.4 hours) and meetings about 3.4 hours lower relative to control. Non-meeting time therefore fell only about 3%.
- Logs, however, show an 11% fall. Taken together with the meeting cut, that implies a total reduction *larger* than timesheets show. This contradicts the claim that logs show "slightly more work than timesheets".

**There is also a problem for the mechanism.** The meetings mechanism people find intuitive is *reallocation*: total hours fall, meetings absorb most of the cut, and time on cases is protected. Earlier I noted the 9-month arithmetic supported this. But if the denominator excludes meetings, reallocation produces *no* gain in output per log-measured hour. A meetings effect on that outcome would then have to work some other way, such as fewer interruptions or better focus. That is a different and less obvious claim.

**If logs measure session time (meetings included while logged in):** the numbers are easier to reconcile. But then logs are not clearly "stricter" than timesheets. They also miss work done off the system, such as phone calls, paper files, or work done without logging in.

**The authors should:**
- define exactly what log time includes;
- reconcile log time, timesheet time and meeting time for each arm;
- explain which mechanism the mediation result supports.

## 2. Two control offices changed practice, and this affects the decline estimate

In month 15, two of the seven control offices ran a "meeting audit". Their output per hour rose by 4.1%. This is contamination of the control group, and the authors treat it only as an interesting aside. It has consequences:

- **It shrinks the difference between treated and control offices.** Better control performance makes the treated advantage look smaller. Some of the apparent fall from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore reflect controls improving, not treated offices fading. The authors should split the change into treated and control trends separately, and re-estimate excluding the two offices or adjusting for the change.
- **It is probably a spillover from the treatment.** Control staff knew about the trial and could see what treated offices had done. An audit prompted by the treatment is a classic spillover effect.
- **It affects the meetings comparison.** The control average at month 24 (7.0 hours) includes two offices at 5.0. That means the other five rose to about 7.8 hours, up from roughly 7.2. The meeting gap between arms then partly reflects meetings creeping up in untouched control offices.

Separately, the decline itself is not statistically tested. The 9-month and 24-month confidence intervals (6.9 to 18.4, and 4.6 to 15.2) overlap heavily. "Consistent with some fading" is a fair description. "Declined by about a quarter", in Section 5, is stated as if it were an established finding.

## 3. "Confirms" overstates the mediation analysis

- **It is not an independent replication.** The exploratory finding came from these same seven treated offices. Registering the test at month 11 rules out choosing the analysis after seeing the 24-month results, which is a real improvement. But testing a hypothesis again on the units that suggested it is weaker than testing it on new units. Varga and Holm's criticism, that the finding was unlikely to replicate, can only be answered by different offices or employers.
- **Office-months are not independent.** The authors cite "a larger sample of office-months". Measurements from the same office are correlated, so the effective sample is still 14 clusters. The interval for the meetings share (28 to 66%) looks narrow for that number. The authors should state how clustering was handled, and whether small-sample corrections were used.
- **The key assumption carries a lot of weight.** Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome (sequential ignorability). Meeting time was not randomised. Offices with stronger managers might cut meetings *and* raise output for other reasons. The Limitations section mentions this, but the Summary says "confirms".
- **The order of mediators affects the split.** Meetings and fatigue are probably correlated, since fewer meetings may mean less fatigue. The 47/18 split depends on how shared variance is allocated, and the authors should report the model's sensitivity to this.

A more accurate summary would be: "A pre-specified mediation analysis in the same offices attributes about half the per-hour gain to reduced meeting time, under standard but untestable assumptions."

## 4. The Summary compares different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". These figures use different hours measures: timesheets for the first, logs for the second. The like-for-like fall is 12.5% to 9.8%, about a fifth in relative terms (ln 1.125 to ln 1.098), not a third. The body text is careful about this; the Summary is not.

## 5. The counter-arm cost figures need a derivation

The arm was closed because treated offices had average waits of 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices. That is a clear and appropriately controlled result. The cost figures, however, don't follow straightforwardly:

- **Staffing.** Actual hours fell 17%, so restoring the same staff presence would need roughly 20% more staff (1 / 0.83). The county's 12% presumably assumes that queues respond non-linearly to staffing, or that the per-hour gain is kept.
- **Cost per contact.** Adding 12% more staff on full pay, while restoring contacts to the control level, implies roughly +12% cost per contact. The +9% figure would need non-staff costs to make up about a quarter of total cost.

Both figures may be reasonable, but the report should show how they were derived.

## 6. The Halden subset

- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the coverage-bound pattern.** The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations". But a marketing agency would be coded as *discretionary* under the meta-analysis's scheme. Client deadlines are a form of availability constraint that a simple discretionary/coverage-bound split doesn't capture. This case shows that the classification is too simple, as the meta-analysis acknowledged, and should be reported that way.
- **The baseline hours figure needs checking.** The baseline of 40.3 hours is the same figure Varga and Holm gave for all 27 time-tracking organisations. The 17-organisation subset was 40.4. Is 40.3 really these 11 organisations' own baseline?
- **"Upper bound" is the wrong term.** The selection is heavy: 14 of 23 organisations responded, and the reverters were removed. The 11.8% is better described as an estimate biased upward by selection, not a formal bound.
- **It can't be compared with the 6-month figure.** The 11.8% here may look like an increase on Varga and Holm's 10.8% at six months, but the two figures come from different subsets. The reverters, with output indices of 88 to 91, have been dropped.

## 7. Questions still open

- **Backlogs and case age.** These are still not reported. At 24 months this is the obvious test of whether staff have been closing easy cases while hard cases age, and the Varden authors themselves flagged backlog build-up as a risk.
- **Overtime cost** is still not reported.
- **No confidence intervals** are given for overturn rates, resignations, the sick-day changes, or the "unexplained 35%".
- **Conflicts of interest.** The authors are judging critiques of their own work. Okafor is a Halden author. Phrases such as "since dismissed as post hoc" read as vindication. In fairness, Varga and Holm's scepticism was reasonable given the evidence at nine months, when the analysis rested on seven offices, was unregistered and had no baseline.

## 8. How this changes the overall picture

**The rebuttals of earlier claims are mostly sound:**
- **Varga and Holm** were wrong that the gain is "entirely an artifact". An 8.5% gain survives randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and two years. But they were partly right about novelty: some fading is plausible, though not proven.
- **The meta-analysis's duration claim.** If its four long studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, that conclusion doesn't stand, as I argued earlier.
- **The coverage-bound finding is now firm.** The county ended the arm rather than accept worse service.

**The evidence now points to:**
- a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% in discretionary public-sector work;
- some decline over two years, with the size uncertain because of control contamination;
- about half the gain plausibly coming from cutting meetings, subject to how log hours are defined.

**The most important question for employers is still open.** It is whether cutting meetings *without* cutting hours would capture most of the gain. The two control offices are suggestive, but they are two offices with no comparison group. The authors are right that only a trial with a reorganisation-only arm can answer it, and that should be the next study.
